pages.title: PYMNTS | ServiceNow Denies Reports of Takeover Interest in Decagon
pages.text:
ServiceNow Denies Reports of Takeover Interest in AI Agent Startup Decagon
ServiceNow denied Tuesday (Oct. 13) media reports suggesting it has shown interest in purchasing Decagon, a developer of artificial intelligence (AI) agents.
Seeking Alpha reported Tuesday (Oct. 13), citing a paywalled article by Business Insider, that Decagon has hired a bank to evaluate purchase interest and has talked with ServiceNow and other companies about a potential sale.
The talks about a potential sale were in their early stages, and a deal may not happen, according to the report.
Decagon did not immediately reply to PYMNTS’ request for comment.
ServiceNow replied to PYMNTS’ request for comment with an emailed statement from Amit Zavery, the company’s president, chief product officer and chief operating officer.
We’d love to be your preferred source for news.
Please add us to your preferred sources list so our news, data and interviews show up in your feed. Thanks!
“We are aware of misinformation in the market today about our acquisition strategy,” Zavery said. “To be clear, ServiceNow has no interest or intention of purchasing Decagon.”
“Our approach to M&A has not changed: we remain an organic growth company first,” Zavery said. “M&A is a tool to accelerate our roadmap or open meaningful new markets, not a substitute for innovation. As we have previously noted, we do not see major strategic gaps that require large-scale acquisitions at this time.”
Decagon announced in a January blog post that it was valued at $4.5 billion in a Series D funding round in which it raised $250 million. The company’s valuation was three times higher than the one it achieved six months earlier, according to the post.
Decagon said that during its previous fiscal year, it gained more than 100 new global enterprise customers for its “concierge approach to product.”
PYMNTS reported in August that Decagon crossed $100 million in annualized revenue three years after launching as a customer service AI startup.
Decagon CEO Jesse Zhang told Newcomer in August that the company’s product is built for a client’s own staff to configure directly and that roughly 90% of Decagon’s workloads run on fine-tuned open-source models rather than frontier models, which the company says are faster and cheaper on narrower, repeatable customer-service tasks.
PYMNTS reported in February that Decagon said one of its partners expanded chat support to 24/7 coverage, increased automated resolution significantly and reported a 95% reduction in cost per support conversation.

ServiceNow Fell 20% Over a Year But This Wall Street Analyst Predicts 70% Gains From Here
ServiceNow's AI business just crossed a major milestone while the stock still sits nearly 20% below where it traded a year ago, and one analyst on Wall Street sees an opportunity the rest of the market is ignoring.
Published October 20, 2026, 10:45am ET · 3 min read
A digital interface featuring a bullish market trend and a symbolic bull, representing active investment and a positive outlook for cryptocurrencies like Hyperliquid (HYPE). © Shutterstock
ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW | NOW Price Prediction) currently trades at $145.33. The average analyst price target is $152.23, which implies 4.7% upside.
ServiceNow sells a cloud platform that automates IT, HR, security and customer workflows, and it now positions itself as the “AI control tower” for large enterprises. Investors are watching because the AI revenue is real: ServiceNow AI crossed $1 billion in annual contract value, and agentic deployments rose 9x in 9 months.
The bigger gap comes from the high end of the Street. Bernstein’s Peter Weed holds an Outperform rating with a $248 target, the highest published. That implies 70.6% upside, a sharp break from where the market prices the stock.
AI Disruption Fears Cut ServiceNow by 58% From Its High
Fear that AI agents would make seat-based software obsolete did most of the damage. Shares fell from a 52-week high of $192.97 to a low of $81.24. That marks a decline of 57.9%. Software stocks entered a bear market in January, and ServiceNow plunged 10% in one session. The sector lost $1 trillion in a week.
ServiceNow added problems of its own. The stock tumbled nearly 15% after management warned that delayed Middle East deals would hit first-quarter subscription growth. Profit also took a hit: second-quarter operating income fell 54.75% to $162M as stock compensation and costs from the Moveworks, Veza and Armis deals piled up. The stock has since climbed 78.9% off its low, yet it is still down 19.58% over the past year.
Bernstein Says the Market Is Underpricing an AI Monetization Engine
Weed’s thesis has three parts. First, Now Assist premium levels expand contract value across existing seats, so AI revenue increases without long new sales cycles. Second, ServiceNow is the default coordination layer for IT, HR and customer workflows. Third, operating leverage should support strong free cash flow margins as subscriptions scale (per Bernstein).
The latest quarter supports that case. Revenue increases 24.0% to $3.987B, and EPS of $0.90 beat the $0.86 consensus, the company’s 4th consecutive beat. Current remaining performance obligations rose 21% to $13.20B, and deals above $1 million increases ~40%. Management’s 2030 targets include $30B+ in subscription revenue and 30% of ACV from AI.
Sentiment is generally positive, but most analysts are far less bullish than Weed. Of 49 analysts, 45 give the stock their top two ratings. Estimates have edged lower: the fiscal 2026 EPS average is at $4.0668, down from $4.1291 90 days ago, while fiscal 2027 stands at $5.0067. A price target is one analyst’s view, and it guarantees nothing.
Software Peers Fell Together, but Recovered Unevenly
The AI disruption trade hit the whole application software group, but each stock has recovered at its own pace.
Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) trades at $242.51. It is up 0.63% over the year but down 7.81% year to date. Its $285.68 consensus target implies 17.8% upside. 38 analysts rate it Buy or better, against 15 Holds.
Workday (NASDAQ:WDAY) trades at $195.20, down 16.67% over the year. Its $207.92 target implies 6.5% upside, and opinion is split: 20 Buy ratings, 19 Holds and 3 Sells.
On consensus targets, Salesforce offers the greatest potential gain among these names. ServiceNow’s case depends on whether Bernstein’s high-end view proves right.
At $145.33, ServiceNow sits 4.7% below its $152.23 consensus target, based on 49 ratings. The stock is down 5.13% year to date and 19.58% over the year. Over the same periods, the S&P 500 rose 12.42% and 15.38%.
Momentum is improving, with a one-month gain of 7.28%. The forward P/E of 28 is far below the trailing multiple of 89.
Why I Lean Bullish but Doubt the Full $248
ServiceNow deserves a closer look here if AI contract value keeps growing and margins rebound once Armis integration costs fade in FY27. But I’d stay cautious if growth slows faster than the guidance suggests. The third-quarter subscription growth guide of 20.5% already reflects federal revenue pulled forward into the second quarter, along with a $35 million currency drag to remaining performance obligations.
I lean bullish. Growth above 20% at 28 times forward earnings looks reasonable for a business that is winning large customers. Still, the consensus target is a more realistic 12-month marker than the 70% call.

ServiceNow (NOW +2.88%) primarily generates its revenue by selling comprehensive cloud-based workflow automation software that helps large enterprises globally streamline their internal information technology, human resources, and customer service operations.

ServiceNow set the date for its third-quarter results during a busy software earnings season.
Enterprise demand for AI-driven workflow tools stayed a central theme across recent commentary.
Software sentiment stayed firm as the market weighed delayed inflation data and rate signals.
ServiceNow, Inc.
moved into sharper focus this week after the enterprise software company set the date for its third-quarter financial results, placing the name squarely within a crowded stretch of software reporting. The scheduling drew fresh attention as the market gauged whether firm demand for AI-driven workflow tools carried through the latest quarter.
The timing matters because the company has become a bellwether for enterprise software spending, with its platform embedded deep inside the operations of many large organizations. Market participants tracking the stock framed the upcoming release as a key read on how businesses are pacing their technology budgets heading into the end of the year.
Fit Into Enterprise Software?
ServiceNow operates a cloud platform that helps large organizations automate workflows across departments, from technology operations to customer service, human resources, and beyond. The system acts as a central layer where tasks, requests, and processes are routed, tracked, and resolved, replacing a patchwork of manual steps and disconnected tools.
That positioning places the company among the most important enterprise software providers, supplying the kind of workflow infrastructure that becomes difficult to remove once adopted. The platform's breadth allows it to expand from a single use case into many across an organization, a pattern that has underpinned the company's steady growth over many years.
What Role Does Earnings Season Play?
The current week sits inside a dense stretch of third-quarter reporting, and enterprise software names have featured prominently in the flow of releases. Earnings season tends to concentrate attention on growth-oriented technology firms, since each report offers a window into enterprise spending patterns and the pace of artificial intelligence adoption.
For a workflow platform such as ServiceNow, the reporting calendar carries extra weight because its subscription-based model offers a clean read on committed enterprise demand. Commentary around new bookings, platform expansion, and AI feature uptake tends to draw close scrutiny as the market gauges the health of corporate technology budgets.
How Is Artificial Intelligence Reshaping Enterprise Workflows?
Artificial intelligence has become a defining theme across enterprise software, and ServiceNow has embedded generative and agentic AI features across its platform under its Now Assist family of tools. These features aim to draft responses, summarize cases, propose next steps, and automate routine work, lifting the productivity of the teams that rely on the system.
The wider adoption wave has lifted demand across enterprise software this year, with organizations seeking tools that turn AI capability into measurable efficiency. For a workflow platform, the appeal is direct, since AI features slot into existing processes and reduce the manual effort behind common tasks, a draw that has featured prominently in recent company commentary.
What Defines the ServiceNow Platform?
At its center, the ServiceNow platform unifies workflows across an organization onto a single system, letting different departments build and run processes without stitching together separate tools. The company started in technology service management and has since expanded across many functions, broadening the platform's reach across the enterprise.
This expansion has been central to the growth story, as customers that adopt the platform for one use case frequently extend it into others. The result is a widening footprint within each account, reinforcing the platform's role as core operational infrastructure rather than a single-purpose application.
How Has Enterprise Demand Been Trending?
Recent commentary has pointed to firm enterprise demand, with the company lifting its full-year guidance on the strength of subscription growth and rising adoption of its AI tools. That strength reflected both new customers and deeper expansion among existing ones, a combination the business has highlighted as a sign of durable demand.
The uptake of AI features has been a particular thread, as more customers adopt the Now Assist tools layered across the platform. This adoption lifts the value each customer draws from the system and ties the business more closely to the broader AI build-out sweeping across enterprise technology budgets.
What Shapes the Competitive Landscape Around ServiceNow
?
The enterprise workflow space is competitive, spanning large cloud providers, enterprise software suites, and specialized tools focused on single functions. ServiceNow competes by offering a unified platform that spans many departments, paired with a growing set of AI features that deepen its usefulness across an organization.
Competition also comes from the largest technology firms, which supply overlapping tools for service management, automation, and AI. Against that backdrop, the company leans on the breadth of its platform, its deep embedding within customer operations, and its track record of expanding across functions to differentiate itself from narrower rivals.
How Do Broader Market Conditions Factor In?
The week unfolded against a macro backdrop marked by delayed inflation data and close attention on the direction of interest rates. Growth-oriented software names tend to react to shifts in rate expectations, since changing financing conditions ripple through how the market weighs businesses built around steady expansion.
ServiceNow sits among the wider group of US Growth Stocks that the market tracks closely during earnings season, and sentiment across that cohort has stayed firm even as macro signals remain mixed. As a member of the S&P 500, the stock also tends to move with broader swings in the technology complex.
What Operational Themes Stand Out?
Operational discipline has featured in the ServiceNow story, with the company pairing durable revenue growth with healthy operating margins. Its subscription model produces a high share of recurring revenue, giving the business a steady base from which to fund continued product development and expansion into new areas.
The company has also emphasized strong renewal rates, a measure of how reliably customers stay on the platform. High retention reinforces the recurring nature of the business and gives management a dependable foundation as it layers new AI features and workflow capabilities onto the existing system.
How Do AI Features Fit the Strategy?
The Now Assist family of AI tools has become a centerpiece of the company's strategy, embedding generative and agentic features across the platform rather than offering them as a separate product. This approach lets AI slot directly into the workflows customers already run, lowering the barrier to adoption.
Early uptake of these features has been a recurring highlight in company commentary, with the business pointing to rising adoption and expanding deals that include AI capabilities. The role of these tools as a layer that lifts productivity across existing processes has reinforced the company's positioning at the forefront of enterprise AI adoption.
What Headwinds Face the Company?
Like other enterprise software firms, ServiceNow faces several headwinds, including sensitivity to corporate technology budgets, longer sales cycles for large deals, and the elevated expectations baked into its share price after a strong run. A pullback in enterprise spending would flow through to the pace of new bookings.
Competition from the largest technology firms and the fast-moving nature of artificial intelligence add further variables. The business must keep extending its platform and AI features to stay ahead, while currency swings and the timing of large contracts can shape results from one quarter to the next.
Sit Within the Broader Market?
ServiceNow ranks among the most closely tracked enterprise software names, and its reports often serve as a reference point for how corporate technology spending is faring. Its moves tend to draw attention across the software complex, reflecting its role as a gauge of enterprise demand and AI adoption.
That broader relevance means the company's commentary carries weight beyond its own customer base, offering a read on workflow automation trends, subscription growth, and the pace at which organizations are embedding AI into daily operations. The upcoming release gives the market a fresh checkpoint on each of those threads.
What Might Shape the Coming Quarters?
Across the coming quarters, the themes most likely to shape the narrative include the pace of subscription growth, the uptake of Now Assist AI features, the expansion of the platform across new functions, and the trajectory of operating margins. Each thread feeds into how the market gauges the durability of the growth story.
The broad push toward enterprise AI adds a near-term layer, since the company stands to benefit as organizations move from pilots toward wider deployments. Commentary tied to AI-linked bookings and platform expansion is expected to stay front and center as the business moves through earnings season and into a new year.
How Does the Subscription Model Support Stability?
At its foundation, the ServiceNow business rests on recurring subscription revenue tied to multi-year contracts. This base provides a steady, predictable stream that gives the company visibility into the pace of its business and cushions it against short-term swings in corporate spending, a quality the market tends to value highly.
The recurring structure also reflects how deeply the platform becomes embedded within customer operations, where ongoing daily use rather than one-time projects drives the relationship. This stability gives management a dependable foundation from which to fund continued development and layer new AI capabilities onto the existing system.
What Is the Role of the Partner Ecosystem?
A broad ecosystem of consulting firms, technology partners, and app builders surrounds the ServiceNow platform, helping customers deploy, customize, and extend it across their operations. This network deepens the platform's usefulness and speeds adoption, since partners bring the expertise needed to tailor the system to complex enterprise needs.
The ecosystem also acts as a growth engine, with partners guiding customers toward wider deployments and building solutions that extend what the platform can do. This model lets the company scale its reach across many industries while keeping its own focus on the core workflow and AI engine at the center of the platform.
How Does International Reach Factor In?
Geographic breadth has grown into a meaningful part of the ServiceNow story, as the company extends its platform across regions and industries around the world. Serving large organizations across many markets diversifies the revenue base and taps into the global push to modernize corporate operations with cloud-based tools.

ServiceNow Stock Rises as Analyst Raises Price Target to $165
ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) shares climbed 1.05% to $141.80 on Tuesday, as Oppenheimer analyst Brian Schwartz raised the price target to $165 from $140. Schwartz cited weak federal obligations in Q3, slower seat growth, and cautious spending as key challenges. He also highlighted ServiceNow’s CRPO guidance, noting the company has historically beaten estimates by 2%. With altcoins to watch gaining attention, the crypto price remains a key focus for traders.
ServiceNow shares rose 1.05% to $141.80 at the time of publication on Tuesday, according to Benzinga Pro. Oppenheimer analyst Brian Schwartz raised the price target to $165 from $140 and reaffirmed an Outperform rating. Oppenheimer's earnings preview examines federal demand and ServiceNow's CRPO.
Schwartz said third-quarter federal obligations to ServiceNow looked weak, providing a negative indication. Slower seat growth following the rationalization of earlier purchases and continued caution about spending probably explain the weakness. Schwartz calculated federal obligations at $424 million as of October 12, down 16% from a year earlier. That level also trails the same period in 2024 and 2023. Schwartz said the year-over-year growth rate trails the three-year average for normal third-quarter patterns by 13 points. Schwartz said the growth rate trails the five-year average by 34 points.
Schwartz described the CRPO picture as mixed. ServiceNow began providing CRPO guidance in 2021. ServiceNow exceeded CRPO guidance by an average of 2%, or $173 million, across the past four quarters. Over three years, the typical third-quarter beat has been 2%, or $193 million. The typical fourth-quarter beat over three years has been 1%, or $92 million.
The third quarter looks easier than the fourth quarter. Wall Street's third-quarter CRPO estimate assumes a $362 million quarter-over-quarter gain. That assumed gain is $51 million below the usual seasonal gain. The estimate also falls $194 million short of what an average seasonal beat would deliver. Management has a long history of exceeding management's guidance. Schwartz expects ServiceNow to exceed consensus, but not by a wide margin. Schwartz expects the beat to be smaller than last quarter's 2% and the 3% recorded a year earlier.
Schwartz sees limited room for fourth-quarter guidance to exceed Wall Street expectations. Schwartz cited weaker federal activity, a harder comparison with last year, demand headwinds and management's cautious approach as constraints. Schwartz also pointed to a shift in AI budgeting. Return on investment now drives scrutiny after a period of broad testing, raising the threshold for each additional dollar of spending. Growth could slow compared with earlier adoption cycles. Schwartz expects less fourth-quarter IT spending than normal because companies allocated budgets earlier, into the first half of 2026, for AI trials.
Schwartz expects ServiceNow to guide fourth-quarter CRPO in line with, or slightly above, the $15.3 billion consensus. That consensus reflects 19% growth from last year.

Should AI Product Wins Require Action From ServiceNow Stock Investors?

ServiceNow has rolled out AI Passport and broader AI governance tools, expanded its EmployeeWorks agent platform, and reported real world deployments with clients like the City of Raleigh and Bundesliga, while also denying interest in acquiring conversational AI startup Decagon.
The new AI Passport authority layer, combined with the Super Intelligence Control Tower and employee built AI agents, points to ServiceNow pushing hard on governed, production grade AI workflows rather than just adding another generic chatbot feature.
We will look at how ServiceNow's AI Passport and governance push feeds into the existing investment narrative around AI driven workflows.
Compare ServiceNow's push into governed AI workflows with other potential beneficiaries by scanning a curated list of 55 AI infrastructure stocks shaping the backbone of enterprise AI adoption.
To own ServiceNow, you largely have to believe that AI driven workflows, security, and CRM can keep deepening its role inside big customers while earnings keep growing faster than revenue. Right now, the key near term swing factor is whether AI native bundles and agentic products keep converting into higher AI ACV after crossing US$1b in Q2 2026.
The biggest operational risk is that heavy reliance on AI workflows and a high margin subscription mix meets either security issues or weaker usage than implied by current adoption figures. The new AI Passport and governance stack directly address that first risk. If customers do not see this as materially improving trust, the impact could be modest.
Among the latest news, AI Passport looks most directly tied to the current thesis. It aims to give enterprises runtime control over AI agents, link those permissions to CMDB and GRC data, and centralize oversight inside the Super Intelligence Control Tower. That is operational plumbing rather than just a feature demo, and it speaks to how ServiceNow wants AI in production rather than limited to pilots.
For investors watching catalysts, this matters because the narrative leans on scaling AI ACV, security workflows, and regulated industry use cases. Making AI agents governed, auditable, and kill switch ready can be particularly important for financial services and public sector wins, where any repeat of past AI platform security flaws would be a clear risk to adoption and subscription momentum.
ServiceNow AI Governance In Context Of Street Assumptions
ServiceNow's push to make AI agents governed and auditable sits against a consensus narrative that still leans heavily on growth forecasts stretching out to 2029 and beyond. Analysts are penciling in relatively specific numbers while the product roadmap is shifting quickly toward supervised agents, AI Passport controls, and more regulated industry workloads.
On the revenue side, the analyst group assumes the business can compound its top line at 19.4% each year for the next three years. That pace effectively underwrites a bigger workflow footprint inside existing customers and a broader reach into areas like security, CRM, and public sector deals where governed AI workflows may matter more than headline features.
Earnings forecasts carry even more detail and a wider band of possible outcomes. The current analyst set expects profit margins to move from 11.3% today to 16.6% in three years. This implies a higher share of high margin subscription activity and some operating leverage from AI driven workflows, while still leaving room for spending on platform security and governance. Consensus calls for earnings to rise from US$1.7b today to US$4.2b by 2029, with the most optimistic forecast at US$5.9b and the most cautious at US$2.7b.
Those earnings assumptions build in a sizeable step up in absolute profit. The move from US$1.7b to US$4.2b would mean an increase of about US$2.5b, even before considering the bullish or bearish edges of the range. For readers tracking what the AI Passport and Super Intelligence Control Tower could mean, the question is less about precision of the earnings path and more about whether controlled, production grade agents can support the margin lift that is baked into these numbers.
Valuation work on ServiceNow then links these operating forecasts to a future earnings multiple. The current analyst framework assumes that by 2029, revenues reach US$25.1b and earnings land at US$4.2b, with the stock trading on a P/E of 47.4x based on those profits. That would be lower than the 85.8x P/E cited today but still above the 30.6x level quoted for the broader US software peer group.
Price targets reflect that tension between strong growth assumptions and already full expectations. The consensus target sits at US$149.93 per share versus a spot price of US$138.61. This implies a 7.5% gap that suggests many analysts view the shares as close to fairly priced on their numbers. The spread between the most bullish target at US$248.00 and the most bearish at US$72.00 shows that investor views around AI execution, security track record, and the durability of workflow demand remain wide.

pages.title: Salesforce Retreats 2% on $5.66B Deal for Braze, Even as ServiceNow and Adobe Gain 2% - 24/7 Wall St.
pages.text:
Salesforce Retreats 2% on $5.66B Deal for Braze, Even as ServiceNow and Adobe Gain 2%
Salesforce just agreed to spend billions in cash on a customer engagement platform, and the market is not applauding. Find out why rivals are rising while Salesforce takes the hit and whether the strategic bet on Marketing Cloud justifies the…
Published October 20, 2026, 9:37am ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
© Noam Galai / Getty Images Entertainment via Getty Images
A large all-cash acquisition is weighing on one of the biggest names in enterprise software. Salesforce (NYSE:CRM | CRM Price Prediction) stock is down 2% to $238.57 in morning trading after the company agreed to buy a customer engagement platform.
Braze (NASDAQ:BRZE) is the Salesforce target, a company that helps consumer brands send personalized messages across channels in real time. Under the terms Salesforce announced, the agreement carries an enterprise value of $5.66 billion, with the full amount payable in cash. Approval from Braze shareholders and regulators is still required, and Salesforce made no change to its current fiscal-year guidance.
That cash spending is the core of the trade-off for Salesforce, set against the boost Braze could give Marketing Cloud, while rival software stocks are mostly holding up, which points to a selloff aimed at Salesforce stock.
Braze Deal Targets Marketing Cloud Personalization
Salesforce expects Braze to strengthen cross-channel personalization inside Marketing Cloud. The company also sees the platform complementing its data and Agentforce products, which anchor its push to build AI agents into every part of its software. Marketing Cloud is the piece of Salesforce’s lineup that stands to change most directly.
Patrick Stokes, Salesforce’s president of applications and marketing, stated that Braze was built to turn live customer behavior into personalized engagement at scale. That description lines up with Salesforce’s customer relationship management software, which gains real-time messaging tools built for consumer brands through the deal.
Braze runs its own BrazeAI suite for AI-powered decisioning and customer journey orchestration. Its technology partnerships with AWS, Snowflake and Databricks could give Salesforce more ways to connect with the data systems its customers already use. Those links matter because Salesforce has framed data as the foundation for its AI products.
Customers on the Braze platform span media and entertainment, financial services, retail and technology. This consumer-facing mix gives Salesforce a deeper foothold with brands that need to reach shoppers and subscribers the moment they engage.
Funding a deal of this scale entirely in cash ties up resources Salesforce could otherwise direct elsewhere, and folding a separate platform into Marketing Cloud adds execution risk that typically extends well past closing.
Supporters of the deal can point to the strategic fit for Salesforce. Braze gives Marketing Cloud a purpose-built engine for real-time engagement, and the same guidance means the purchase doesn’t alter management’s current fiscal-year outlook.
Even as CRM stock slips, ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) stock is up 2% to $148.10. Furthermore, Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) stock is up 2% to $252.47.
The business overlap with Salesforce differs for Adobe and ServiceNow. Marketing software is where Adobe competes with Salesforce, putting it closest to the territory Braze covers. Workflow automation software is ServiceNow’s business, which sits further from the marketing fight.
For a sector read against Salesforce, the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (CBOE:IGV) is down 0.3% to $105.65. Large-cap tech is a touch softer as well, with a NASDAQ 100 tracking fund down 0.5% to $715.16. A modest dip in the software fund next to the sharper drop in Salesforce stock marks the selloff as specific to the company.
Investors are now watching whether regulators clear the Braze deal on schedule. Braze shareholders must also approve the agreement before it can close, and any delay in either review could keep pressure on Salesforce stock.
Until the deal closes and integration progress is visible, Salesforce stock investors should keep their positions moderate. Steady rival software stocks point to deal-specific risk rather than a sector problem, which supports a conservative approach to adding shares.

pages.title: ServiceNow's Analyst Targets Rise in Unison, but Conviction Doesn't Follow
pages.text:
Sie befinden sich hier: Startseite > Börse > Unternehmensnachrichten > ServiceNow s Analyst Targets Rise in Unison, but Conviction Dösn ...
ServiceNow Inc. (US81762P1021) Flatlay zeigt Aktienzertifikat, ISIN-Karte US81762P1021 und Workflow-Notizbuch auf einem Holzschreibtisch Illustration mit AI erstellt.
ServiceNow drew two distinct strands of news this week — one from the analyst community, one from the customer front — and they tell slightly different stories about how far the company's AI narrative has actually traveled.
On October 6, both Stifel and UBS lifted their price targets on the stock. Stifel moved from $120 to $160 while keeping its buy rating intact. UBS went from $110 to $150 but stayed at "neutral." The symmetry ends there. Two houses, two higher targets, two very different levels of enthusiasm — a reminder that a raised target and a buy call are not the same thing, and investors are better served reading both halves of any analyst note together.
What the two firms did not do was explain their moves in a way that can be pinned to a single shared catalyst. ServiceNow's recent customer and product disclosures form an operational backdrop, but they don't substitute for the analysts' own reasoning.
The more tangible thread came on Thursday, when ServiceNow disclosed that the City of Raleigh has put its IT Service Desk AI Specialist into production. According to the company, the deployment cut IT service desk costs by 66%, with nearly half of all IT support requests resolved autonomously.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying ServiceNow?
That is a sharper data point than a feature announcement — the benefit is anchored to a measurable operational outcome rather than a promise. Still, it is one deployment. Nothing in it guarantees similar savings at other customers, nor does it translate directly into a specific effect on ServiceNow's revenue or earnings. Treating the Raleigh result as proof of a broad-based commercial breakthrough overreaches. As evidence that AI can deliver quantifiable value in day-to-day operations, it holds up.
A day earlier, on Wednesday, ServiceNow said the Bundesliga had selected it as official CRM partner, extending a relationship that already had the company serving as official workflow partner. The league reported that 89% of fan inquiries were resolved on first contact after consolidating seven digital channels.
That figure speaks to the strength of the customer engagement described — but it should not be read as an already-realized result of the newly announced CRM partnership. The more meaningful signal is structural: broadening an existing collaboration is a concrete step, and it carries more weight than a general promise about future capabilities.
ServiceNow also rolled out AI Workflow Factory and Autonomous Engineer on October 6. The tools are designed to identify AI workflow opportunities and to support the build-out and operation of AI workflows inside enterprises. AI Workflow Factory was generally available worldwide at launch. Autonomous Engineer was offered through early access.
For investors, that gap matters. General availability and early access represent different stages of maturity, and the two offerings shouldn't be treated as equally proven. New tools widen the runway, but an announcement by itself doesn't answer questions about adoption or economic return.
ServiceNow at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now.
The broader market backdrop deserves its own clear-eyed treatment. Reuters reported on October 6 that earnings expectations were rising and that fears of AI-driven displacement in the software sector were easing — with ServiceNow among the companies supporting that recovery. That explains a more favorable environment; it does not establish what triggered any given day's move.
ServiceNow has said it will report third-quarter 2026 results after the close on October 28, 2026. That date is the next scheduled opportunity to square the product and customer story with the financials.
Until then, higher analyst targets sit alongside divergent recommendations. The customer wins make the practical value of ServiceNow's applications tangible. What they mean for the company's economics cannot be inferred from individual deployments alone. The verdict leans cautiously positive: real-world use cases and an expanded customer relationship add substance to the AI story, but they are not yet enough to settle the central valuation question — whether operational progress shows up in durable financial results.

ServiceNow Research Study Warns Security Leaders: Ungoverned Agentic AI Exposure Is Compounding Inside Enterprises
Tue, October 20, 2026 at 8:00 AM CDT 4 min read
90% of organizations worldwide already had an agentic AI security incident in the last year, finds new research surveying 3,700+ global security leaders
Only 13% of businesses have a defensible security posture; ServiceNow calls on enterprises to close the gap between AI chaos and AI control
SANTA CLARA, Calif., October 20, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--ServiceNow (NYSE: NOW), the Super Intelligence Control Tower for business reinvention, today warned that ungoverned agentic AI exposure is compounding inside the enterprise, based on new global research of senior security leaders. The warning comes as AI agents move out of pilots and into the systems that run hospitals, airports, factory floors, financial institutions, and beyond. Environments where a single ungoverned action can mean devastating impacts on society. Nine in ten global organizations have already experienced an agentic AI security incident in the past year, and only 36% of those businesses contained it in under 24 hours.
"The agentic incidents making headlines this year are a warning about what can happen when AI is deployed without the right controls," said Ben de Bont, CISO, ServiceNow. "Organizations shouldn't have to choose between moving quickly and managing risk. The ones that get this right will build governance into how they deploy agents from the start, so they can realize the benefits of AI without losing visibility or control."
Inside the AI chaos: what the research found
According to Deployed but ungoverned: the state of agentic security, while many security leaders self-assess as having established agentic security postures, only 13% have defensible programs when measured against five key domains: attack surface, accountability, security by design, visibility, and audit readiness.
Most agentic AI is currently governed by legacy frameworks and human-driven systems, with less than half of organizations using governance frameworks that cover key elements of AI agent deployments. Just 44% of security teams globally design security into an agent's development before it's built, which means for the majority, permissions and guardrails are being implemented on an ad-hoc, after-the-fact basis. That's reactive by design.
Scale and blind spots compound organizations' exposure
Forty-nine percent of organizations now run between 100 and 999 AI agents, and 35% run more than 1,000.
Fifty-seven percent of security teams have a full, accurate record of every AI agent in production and have processes to track changes.
Twenty-nine percent of security teams found AI agents running in production that had never been registered or known. What gets missed can surface later as shadow AI, discovered only after it's already been running unsupervised.
Machine-speed risk is outpacing human-speed response
Seventy-six percent of organizations say they maintain a complete, current map of every agent's access, but only 19% can see more than 90% of their agents in real time.
Even organizations that can see a problem often can't stop it fast enough. Two-thirds (66%) cannot act automatically when an agent behaves anomalously, which means a human still has to intervene before anything changes.
ServiceNow's Autonomous Security offering helps move companies from reactive, fragmented security to enable prevention-first, autonomously governed security that can operate faster than AI creates risk. Operating on the Shift Zero imperative, ServiceNow is supporting organizations to achieve as close to zero exposure at all times as possible, enabling enterprises to answer, with proof, what systems are doing, why, and who/what is accountable, while AI moves as fast as the business needs. This includes the rules and guardrails to safely adopt agentic AI, including a kill switch and AI Passport.
"Innovation and security have to move together, not in sequence," said Nadir Izrael, GVP, Cybersecurity and Risk, ServiceNow. "That's what Autonomous Security and Shift Zero are built for: governance embedded the moment an agent is built or deployed, not bolted on after. Security that runs at machine speed stops being the brake on AI adoption and becomes what makes scaling it safe."
Deployed but ungoverned: the state of agentic security was conducted by ServiceNow in conjunction with Phronesis Partners. The study surveyed more than 3,700 senior security and technology decision-makers, VP level and above, across 20 countries. Respondents represent midsize and large organizations, with 97% reporting annual revenue of $250M or more.

The share price still trails that progress. Our high confidence comes from steady performance: ServiceNow has beaten revenue and EPS estimates in each of the six quarters in our data.
A 24% Revenue Quarter Is Pulling Shares Off the Lows
The stock gained 0.93% over the past week and 5.08% over the past month. It is still down 9.09% year to date and 24.62% over the past year. Over the past 52 weeks it has traded between $81.24 and $192.97.
Second-quarter revenue came in at $3.987B, +24% YoY, above the $3.927B estimate. Non-GAAP EPS of $0.90 topped the $0.8564 consensus. Current remaining performance obligations (cRPO, contracted revenue due within 12 months) reached $13.20B, and the renewal rate held at 98%.
AI monetization is accelerating. AI net new ACV grew over 40% quarter over quarter, and million-dollar-plus AI deals tripled. Price uplifts on the ProPlus tier remain above 30%. Level 1 AI agents are closing 80 to 85% of service requests with no human involvement.
Cybersecurity, strengthened by the Armis and Veza acquisitions, is already a billion-dollar-plus business. Bill McDermott, ServiceNow’s chief executive, called this “the foundation for a re-rating of ServiceNow.”
Most analysts on Wall Street agree: 10 analysts rate the stock a strong buy and 35 rate it a buy. In the bull case, the stock reaches $273.09, a 97.02% return.
GAAP operating income fell to $162M (-54.75% YoY), and GAAP subscription gross margin slipped to 73.5% from 80%. Some of Q2’s strength came from U.S. Federal revenue pulled forward from Q3. Q3 subscription growth is guided to slow to about 20.5%, and currency changes will cut about $35M from Q3 cRPO.
That said, most of the GAAP pressure comes from amortization of acquired intangibles and stock-based compensation linked to the acquisitions. Non-GAAP subscription gross margin is guided at 81%, and free cash flow rose to $634M, +20.5% YoY. Our bear case of $194.48 still sits above today’s price.
ServiceNow Grows Faster Than Salesforce and Workday
Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) is a direct rival now that ServiceNow runs a 2 billion ACV CRM business. Salesforce grew revenue 10.83% last quarter and trades at 26x trailing earnings, while Agentforce ARR climbed over 240%. ServiceNow’s 30x forward multiple is a modest premium for much faster growth, which makes our target look reasonable.
Workday (NASDAQ:WDAY) competes with ServiceNow’s EmployeeWorks for HR workflows. Workday trades at 53x trailing earnings on 12.82% revenue growth, with a 31.1% non-GAAP operating margin. Next to Workday, our target looks conservative.
AI Monetization Tips the Scale Toward a Buy Rating
Our 24/7 Wall St. price target of $246.50 carries a buy rating at 90% confidence. The key factor is AI growing from a pilot program into a source of ACV.
The bull case strengthens if AI ACV remains on track to beat one and a half billion by year-end. The case weakens if Q3 cRPO growth falls short of guidance. Today, the growth figures support the buy rating.
Here is where our model projects ServiceNow would trade if prevailing trends persist.
Price Target from 24/7 Wall St.
These estimates assume ServiceNow continues executing toward its $30B+ subscription revenue target for 2030. Results could land well above or below these levels depending on how fast AI pricing scales and how smoothly Armis is integrated.

Enterprise Software Stocks Fall as AI Financing Worries Spread: Palantir and ServiceNow Drop 5%, Salesforce Slides 4%
Palantir, ServiceNow, and Salesforce are sliding hard as investors turn skeptical about who actually pays for the AI buildout powering their growth, and the answer could reshape how the entire software sector gets valued.
Published October 16, 2026, 11:57am ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
A digital stock chart displays a mix of green uptrends and red downtrends, reflecting the fluctuating nature of financial markets and individual stock performance. © Thinkstock
Enterprise software is taking the brunt of a fresh pullback in AI-linked stocks, and some of the sector’s biggest names are leading the way lower. Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR | PLTR Price Prediction) shares have slipped 5%, recently changing hands at $190.28.
Meanwhile, ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) stock is down 5% to $141.68, in line with the slide in Palantir shares. Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) stock is down 4% to $238.06, marking a slightly smaller decline than Palantir stock and ServiceNow stock are posting.
The selling is notable within the software group. The iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (CBOE:IGV) is down 4%, landing in the same range as Palantir stock, ServiceNow stock and Salesforce stock. Meanwhile, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 1.35%, representing a softer pullback for large-cap tech.
This decline extends a rotation out of AI-linked stocks as investors question how AI infrastructure spending gets financed. Palantir, ServiceNow and Salesforce all sell software that benefits from that spending, so doubts about its funding feed directly into the pricing of Palantir stock, ServiceNow stock and Salesforce stock.
ServiceNow added a company-specific development on Wednesday, stating that it has no interest or intention of purchasing Decagon, a maker of AI customer-service agents, and that it prioritizes organic growth. Management’s stance keeps ServiceNow focused on building out its own AI agent products in-house. Decagon is privately held, so ServiceNow’s statement doesn’t point to any other listed company.
Palantir sells data analytics and AI software to government and commercial clients through Gotham, Foundry and its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP). Gotham serves government customers, Foundry targets commercial users, and AIP helps organizations put AI to work inside their operations. Its pitch centers on AI sovereignty, the idea that customers can deploy AI while keeping full control of their data.
ServiceNow sells workflow software and Salesforce sells customer-relationship software, both on recurring subscriptions with their own AI agent products. On the product side, ServiceNow’s AI Control Tower governs and deploys enterprise AI agents, while Salesforce builds its pitch around Agentforce. Those subscription models give ServiceNow and Salesforce steadier revenue, yet ServiceNow stock and Salesforce stock are sliding with the rest of the AI-linked group.
Palantir’s bullish thesis rests on its government and commercial AI demand. Palantir serves U.S. defense, intelligence and civilian agencies, international governments and a rapidly expanding base of U.S. commercial enterprises. That diversity gives Palantir more than one source of AI spending to draw from as customers build out their own systems.
The skeptics could read the selloff differently. In the bear case, software tied to AI spending is being marked down with the rest of the AI trade, and Palantir stock has little cushion when sentiment turns. Despite strong customer demand, Palantir shares are falling alongside ServiceNow stock and Salesforce stock.
AI Financing Fears Test Software Premiums
Investors should watch to see if the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF narrows its gap with the Invesco QQQ Trust, which could signal that the software rotation is easing. Palantir’s government and commercial AI demand gives the company a fundamental anchor while that rotation plays out.
The open variable for Palantir, ServiceNow and Salesforce is the depth of the rotation out of AI-linked stocks, with ServiceNow also committed to organic growth after its Decagon statement. A conservative approach fits a selloff driven by financing concerns across the AI trade, so owners of Palantir stock, ServiceNow stock and Salesforce stock should keep their position sizes moderate.

ServiceNow Climbs 5% After Denying Decagon Acquisition Interest; Salesforce Rises 4%, Palantir Dips
A flat denial from ServiceNow's president sent the stock surging, but the real question is whether shutting down acquisition rumors actually strengthens the company's position in a market crowded with AI rivals building the exact tools it claims not to…
Published October 15, 2026, 12:58pm ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
An engineer utilizes sophisticated design software, similar to platforms offered by Cadence Design Systems, to develop complex chips essential for advancing AI technologies. This detailed work is crucial for the AI buildout discussed in the article. © gorodenkoff / iStock via Getty Images
A flat denial of takeover talk is lifting one of the biggest names in enterprise software. ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW | NOW Price Prediction) stock is up 5% to $146.93 in midday trading after the company rejected reports that it planned to buy Decagon, a privately held maker of artificial intelligence (AI) customer-service agents.
Meanwhile, Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) stock is up 4% to $245.39, a gain just shy of the advance in ServiceNow stock. Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) stock is down 0.9% to $199.07, moving opposite both of those software gainers. That split points to selective buying inside the enterprise software group.
ServiceNow moved to shut down the speculation on October 14. Amit Zavery, the company’s president, chief product officer and chief operating officer, stated, “We are aware of misinformation in the market today about our acquisition strategy. To be clear, ServiceNow has no interest or intention of purchasing Decagon.” Zavery added that the approach to acquisitions is unchanged and that ServiceNow prioritizes organic growth.
Management also sees no major strategic gaps requiring large-scale deals at this time, according to Zavery. Because ServiceNow sells workflow software on recurring subscriptions, the denial of a big acquisition signals where ServiceNow’s margins and product roadmap could be heading, and organic growth tends to keep spending tied to products ServiceNow controls end to end.
Home-grown agent tools already sit inside the ServiceNow lineup, including AI Control Tower for governing enterprise agents, Now Assist and Build Agent. That catalog gives ServiceNow an internal path into customer-service automation, the niche where Decagon competes.
Sector funds are splitting along the same line as ServiceNow stock and Palantir stock. For a sector read, the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (CBOE:IGV) is up 0.9% to $108.65, a far smaller gain than the move in ServiceNow stock. Across large-cap technology, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 0.7% to $723.84, sliding in the same direction as Palantir stock.
Holders of both the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF and the Invesco QQQ Trust are seeing their portfolios pulled in opposite directions. Because Palantir is a component of the Invesco QQQ Trust, the dip in Palantir stock and the fund’s decline land on the same side of the ledger.
On the bullish side, ServiceNow’s subscription model and its stated focus on organic growth could protect the margins that steady revenue supports, and skipping a large deal keeps management’s attention on shipping its own agent products. Recurring contracts give ServiceNow a predictable base that a big acquisition might have complicated.
However, a denial removes a rumor without adding new revenue for ServiceNow, and headline-driven gains can fade once the news moves on. Startups building AI customer-service agents, Decagon among them, show how crowded the ServiceNow corner of the market is becoming.
Salesforce offers a parallel story. Bulls see its Agentforce platform as proof that organic agent products can win customers, though bears may note today’s gain rests on sympathy rather than company-specific news. Palantir differs from both. Bulls point to its data-analytics strength with government and commercial clients, while bears argue its far higher valuation leaves room for more profit-taking on crowded agentic AI headlines (we profiled seven companies driving the AI expansion beyond the chipmakers in a free report here).
ServiceNow currently faces the question of whether organic product releases carry the roadmap the company says it doesn’t need deals to fill. Zavery’s comments set that bar publicly, which gives each product launch more weight in the debate over ServiceNow stock. Customer adoption of the existing agent lineup may offer the clearest early evidence.
Salesforce and Palantir face tests of their own. Salesforce must show its agent products keep drawing customers once the sympathy rally cools off, while Palantir must defend its premium as rivals crowd the agentic AI field. The takeaway: investors should keep their positions in ServiceNow stock moderate until adoption evidence arrives, and watch for whether gains broaden across the software group.

Enterprise demand for AI-driven workflow tools stayed a central theme across recent commentary.
Software sentiment stayed firm as the market weighed delayed inflation data and rate signals.
ServiceNow, Inc.
moved into sharper focus this week after the enterprise software company set the date for its third-quarter financial results, placing the name squarely within a crowded stretch of software reporting. The scheduling drew fresh attention as the market gauged whether firm demand for AI-driven workflow tools carried through the latest quarter.
The timing matters because the company has become a bellwether for enterprise software spending, with its platform embedded deep inside the operations of many large organizations. Market participants tracking the stock framed the upcoming release as a key read on how businesses are pacing their technology budgets heading into the end of the year.
Fit Into Enterprise Software?
ServiceNow operates a cloud platform that helps large organizations automate workflows across departments, from technology operations to customer service, human resources, and beyond. The system acts as a central layer where tasks, requests, and processes are routed, tracked, and resolved, replacing a patchwork of manual steps and disconnected tools.
That positioning places the company among the most important enterprise software providers, supplying the kind of workflow infrastructure that becomes difficult to remove once adopted. The platform's breadth allows it to expand from a single use case into many across an organization, a pattern that has underpinned the company's steady growth over many years.
What Role Does Earnings Season Play?
The current week sits inside a dense stretch of third-quarter reporting, and enterprise software names have featured prominently in the flow of releases. Earnings season tends to concentrate attention on growth-oriented technology firms, since each report offers a window into enterprise spending patterns and the pace of artificial intelligence adoption.
For a workflow platform such as ServiceNow, the reporting calendar carries extra weight because its subscription-based model offers a clean read on committed enterprise demand. Commentary around new bookings, platform expansion, and AI feature uptake tends to draw close scrutiny as the market gauges the health of corporate technology budgets.
How Is Artificial Intelligence Reshaping Enterprise Workflows?
Artificial intelligence has become a defining theme across enterprise software, and ServiceNow has embedded generative and agentic AI features across its platform under its Now Assist family of tools. These features aim to draft responses, summarize cases, propose next steps, and automate routine work, lifting the productivity of the teams that rely on the system.
The wider adoption wave has lifted demand across enterprise software this year, with organizations seeking tools that turn AI capability into measurable efficiency. For a workflow platform, the appeal is direct, since AI features slot into existing processes and reduce the manual effort behind common tasks, a draw that has featured prominently in recent company commentary.
What Defines the ServiceNow Platform?
At its center, the ServiceNow platform unifies workflows across an organization onto a single system, letting different departments build and run processes without stitching together separate tools. The company started in technology service management and has since expanded across many functions, broadening the platform's reach across the enterprise.
This expansion has been central to the growth story, as customers that adopt the platform for one use case frequently extend it into others. The result is a widening footprint within each account, reinforcing the platform's role as core operational infrastructure rather than a single-purpose application.
How Has Enterprise Demand Been Trending?
Recent commentary has pointed to firm enterprise demand, with the company lifting its full-year guidance on the strength of subscription growth and rising adoption of its AI tools. That strength reflected both new customers and deeper expansion among existing ones, a combination the business has highlighted as a sign of durable demand.
The uptake of AI features has been a particular thread, as more customers adopt the Now Assist tools layered across the platform. This adoption lifts the value each customer draws from the system and ties the business more closely to the broader AI build-out sweeping across enterprise technology budgets.
What Shapes the Competitive Landscape Around ServiceNow
?
The enterprise workflow space is competitive, spanning large cloud providers, enterprise software suites, and specialized tools focused on single functions. ServiceNow competes by offering a unified platform that spans many departments, paired with a growing set of AI features that deepen its usefulness across an organization.
Competition also comes from the largest technology firms, which supply overlapping tools for service management, automation, and AI. Against that backdrop, the company leans on the breadth of its platform, its deep embedding within customer operations, and its track record of expanding across functions to differentiate itself from narrower rivals.
How Do Broader Market Conditions Factor In?
The week unfolded against a macro backdrop marked by delayed inflation data and close attention on the direction of interest rates. Growth-oriented software names tend to react to shifts in rate expectations, since changing financing conditions ripple through how the market weighs businesses built around steady expansion.
ServiceNow sits among the wider group of US Growth Stocks that the market tracks closely during earnings season, and sentiment across that cohort has stayed firm even as macro signals remain mixed. As a member of the S&P 500, the stock also tends to move with broader swings in the technology complex.
What Operational Themes Stand Out?
Operational discipline has featured in the ServiceNow story, with the company pairing durable revenue growth with healthy operating margins. Its subscription model produces a high share of recurring revenue, giving the business a steady base from which to fund continued product development and expansion into new areas.
The company has also emphasized strong renewal rates, a measure of how reliably customers stay on the platform. High retention reinforces the recurring nature of the business and gives management a dependable foundation as it layers new AI features and workflow capabilities onto the existing system.
How Do AI Features Fit the Strategy?
The Now Assist family of AI tools has become a centerpiece of the company's strategy, embedding generative and agentic features across the platform rather than offering them as a separate product. This approach lets AI slot directly into the workflows customers already run, lowering the barrier to adoption.
Early uptake of these features has been a recurring highlight in company commentary, with the business pointing to rising adoption and expanding deals that include AI capabilities. The role of these tools as a layer that lifts productivity across existing processes has reinforced the company's positioning at the forefront of enterprise AI adoption.
What Headwinds Face the Company?
Like other enterprise software firms, ServiceNow faces several headwinds, including sensitivity to corporate technology budgets, longer sales cycles for large deals, and the elevated expectations baked into its share price after a strong run. A pullback in enterprise spending would flow through to the pace of new bookings.
Competition from the largest technology firms and the fast-moving nature of artificial intelligence add further variables. The business must keep extending its platform and AI features to stay ahead, while currency swings and the timing of large contracts can shape results from one quarter to the next.
Sit Within the Broader Market?
ServiceNow ranks among the most closely tracked enterprise software names, and its reports often serve as a reference point for how corporate technology spending is faring. Its moves tend to draw attention across the software complex, reflecting its role as a gauge of enterprise demand and AI adoption.
That broader relevance means the company's commentary carries weight beyond its own customer base, offering a read on workflow automation trends, subscription growth, and the pace at which organizations are embedding AI into daily operations. The upcoming release gives the market a fresh checkpoint on each of those threads.
What Might Shape the Coming Quarters?
Across the coming quarters, the themes most likely to shape the narrative include the pace of subscription growth, the uptake of Now Assist AI features, the expansion of the platform across new functions, and the trajectory of operating margins. Each thread feeds into how the market gauges the durability of the growth story.
The broad push toward enterprise AI adds a near-term layer, since the company stands to benefit as organizations move from pilots toward wider deployments. Commentary tied to AI-linked bookings and platform expansion is expected to stay front and center as the business moves through earnings season and into a new year.
How Does the Subscription Model Support Stability?
At its foundation, the ServiceNow business rests on recurring subscription revenue tied to multi-year contracts. This base provides a steady, predictable stream that gives the company visibility into the pace of its business and cushions it against short-term swings in corporate spending, a quality the market tends to value highly.
The recurring structure also reflects how deeply the platform becomes embedded within customer operations, where ongoing daily use rather than one-time projects drives the relationship. This stability gives management a dependable foundation from which to fund continued development and layer new AI capabilities onto the existing system.
What Is the Role of the Partner Ecosystem?
A broad ecosystem of consulting firms, technology partners, and app builders surrounds the ServiceNow platform, helping customers deploy, customize, and extend it across their operations. This network deepens the platform's usefulness and speeds adoption, since partners bring the expertise needed to tailor the system to complex enterprise needs.
The ecosystem also acts as a growth engine, with partners guiding customers toward wider deployments and building solutions that extend what the platform can do. This model lets the company scale its reach across many industries while keeping its own focus on the core workflow and AI engine at the center of the platform.
How Does International Reach Factor In?
Geographic breadth has grown into a meaningful part of the ServiceNow story, as the company extends its platform across regions and industries around the world. Serving large organizations across many markets diversifies the revenue base and taps into the global push to modernize corporate operations with cloud-based tools.
International growth also broadens the pool of enterprises that can adopt the platform, from government bodies to financial institutions and manufacturers. The new AI Passport authority layer, combined with the Super Intelligence Control Tower and employee built AI agents, points to ServiceNow pushing hard on governed, production grade AI workflows rather than just adding another generic chatbot feature.

A large all-cash acquisition is weighing on one of the biggest names in enterprise software. Salesforce (NYSE:CRM | CRM Price Prediction) stock is down 2% to $238.57 in morning trading after the company agreed to buy a customer engagement platform.
Braze (NASDAQ:BRZE) is the Salesforce target, a company that helps consumer brands send personalized messages across channels in real time. Under the terms Salesforce announced, the agreement carries an enterprise value of $5.66 billion, with the full amount payable in cash. Approval from Braze shareholders and regulators is still required, and Salesforce made no change to its current fiscal-year guidance.
That cash spending is the core of the trade-off for Salesforce, set against the boost Braze could give Marketing Cloud, while rival software stocks are mostly holding up, which points to a selloff aimed at Salesforce stock.
Braze Deal Targets Marketing Cloud Personalization
Salesforce expects Braze to strengthen cross-channel personalization inside Marketing Cloud. The company also sees the platform complementing its data and Agentforce products, which anchor its push to build AI agents into every part of its software. Marketing Cloud is the piece of Salesforce’s lineup that stands to change most directly.
Patrick Stokes, Salesforce’s president of applications and marketing, stated that Braze was built to turn live customer behavior into personalized engagement at scale. That description lines up with Salesforce’s customer relationship management software, which gains real-time messaging tools built for consumer brands through the deal.
Braze runs its own BrazeAI suite for AI-powered decisioning and customer journey orchestration. Its technology partnerships with AWS, Snowflake and Databricks could give Salesforce more ways to connect with the data systems its customers already use. Those links matter because Salesforce has framed data as the foundation for its AI products.
Customers on the Braze platform span media and entertainment, financial services, retail and technology. This consumer-facing mix gives Salesforce a deeper foothold with brands that need to reach shoppers and subscribers the moment they engage.
Funding a deal of this scale entirely in cash ties up resources Salesforce could otherwise direct elsewhere, and folding a separate platform into Marketing Cloud adds execution risk that typically extends well past closing.
Supporters of the deal can point to the strategic fit for Salesforce. Braze gives Marketing Cloud a purpose-built engine for real-time engagement, and the same guidance means the purchase doesn’t alter management’s current fiscal-year outlook.
Even as CRM stock slips, ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) stock is up 2% to $148.10. Furthermore, Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) stock is up 2% to $252.47.
The business overlap with Salesforce differs for Adobe and ServiceNow. Marketing software is where Adobe competes with Salesforce, putting it closest to the territory Braze covers. Workflow automation software is ServiceNow’s business, which sits further from the marketing fight.
For a sector read against Salesforce, the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (CBOE:IGV) is down 0.3% to $105.65. Large-cap tech is a touch softer as well, with a NASDAQ 100 tracking fund down 0.5% to $715.16. A modest dip in the software fund next to the sharper drop in Salesforce stock marks the selloff as specific to the company.
Investors are now watching whether regulators clear the Braze deal on schedule. Braze shareholders must also approve the agreement before it can close, and any delay in either review could keep pressure on Salesforce stock.
Until the deal closes and integration progress is visible, Salesforce stock investors should keep their positions moderate. Steady rival software stocks point to deal-specific risk rather than a sector problem, which supports a conservative approach to adding shares.

ServiceNow drew two distinct strands of news this week — one from the analyst community, one from the customer front — and they tell slightly different stories about how far the company's AI narrative has actually traveled.
On October 6, both Stifel and UBS lifted their price targets on the stock. Stifel moved from $120 to $160 while keeping its buy rating intact. UBS went from $110 to $150 but stayed at "neutral." The symmetry ends there. Two houses, two higher targets, two very different levels of enthusiasm — a reminder that a raised target and a buy call are not the same thing, and investors are better served reading both halves of any analyst note together.
What the two firms did not do was explain their moves in a way that can be pinned to a single shared catalyst. ServiceNow's recent customer and product disclosures form an operational backdrop, but they don't substitute for the analysts' own reasoning.
The more tangible thread came on Thursday, when ServiceNow disclosed that the City of Raleigh has put its IT Service Desk AI Specialist into production. According to the company, the deployment cut IT service desk costs by 66%, with nearly half of all IT support requests resolved autonomously.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying ServiceNow?
That is a sharper data point than a feature announcement — the benefit is anchored to a measurable operational outcome rather than a promise. Still, it is one deployment. Nothing in it guarantees similar savings at other customers, nor does it translate directly into a specific effect on ServiceNow's revenue or earnings. Treating the Raleigh result as proof of a broad-based commercial breakthrough overreaches. As evidence that AI can deliver quantifiable value in day-to-day operations, it holds up.
A day earlier, on Wednesday, ServiceNow said the Bundesliga had selected it as official CRM partner, extending a relationship that already had the company serving as official workflow partner. The league reported that 89% of fan inquiries were resolved on first contact after consolidating seven digital channels.
That figure speaks to the strength of the customer engagement described — but it should not be read as an already-realized result of the newly announced CRM partnership. The more meaningful signal is structural: broadening an existing collaboration is a concrete step, and it carries more weight than a general promise about future capabilities.
ServiceNow also rolled out AI Workflow Factory and Autonomous Engineer on October 6. The tools are designed to identify AI workflow opportunities and to support the build-out and operation of AI workflows inside enterprises. AI Workflow Factory was generally available worldwide at launch. Autonomous Engineer was offered through early access.
For investors, that gap matters. General availability and early access represent different stages of maturity, and the two offerings shouldn't be treated as equally proven. New tools widen the runway, but an announcement by itself doesn't answer questions about adoption or economic return.
ServiceNow at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now.
The broader market backdrop deserves its own clear-eyed treatment. Reuters reported on October 6 that earnings expectations were rising and that fears of AI-driven displacement in the software sector were easing — with ServiceNow among the companies supporting that recovery. That explains a more favorable environment; it does not establish what triggered any given day's move.
ServiceNow has said it will report third-quarter 2026 results after the close on October 28, 2026. That date is the next scheduled opportunity to square the product and customer story with the financials.
Until then, higher analyst targets sit alongside divergent recommendations. The customer wins make the practical value of ServiceNow's applications tangible. What they mean for the company's economics cannot be inferred from individual deployments alone. The verdict leans cautiously positive: real-world use cases and an expanded customer relationship add substance to the AI story, but they are not yet enough to settle the central valuation question — whether operational progress shows up in durable financial results.

Seventy-six percent of organizations say they maintain a complete, current map of every agent's access, but only 19% can see more than 90% of their agents in real time.

Published October 16, 2026, 11:57am ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
A digital stock chart displays a mix of green uptrends and red downtrends, reflecting the fluctuating nature of financial markets and individual stock performance. © Thinkstock
Enterprise software is taking the brunt of a fresh pullback in AI-linked stocks, and some of the sector’s biggest names are leading the way lower. Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR | PLTR Price Prediction) shares have slipped 5%, recently changing hands at $190.28.
Meanwhile, ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) stock is down 5% to $141.68, in line with the slide in Palantir shares. Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) stock is down 4% to $238.06, marking a slightly smaller decline than Palantir stock and ServiceNow stock are posting.
The selling is notable within the software group. The iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (CBOE:IGV) is down 4%, landing in the same range as Palantir stock, ServiceNow stock and Salesforce stock. Meanwhile, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is down 1.35%, representing a softer pullback for large-cap tech.
This decline extends a rotation out of AI-linked stocks as investors question how AI infrastructure spending gets financed. Palantir, ServiceNow and Salesforce all sell software that benefits from that spending, so doubts about its funding feed directly into the pricing of Palantir stock, ServiceNow stock and Salesforce stock.
ServiceNow added a company-specific development on Wednesday, stating that it has no interest or intention of purchasing Decagon, a maker of AI customer-service agents, and that it prioritizes organic growth. Management’s stance keeps ServiceNow focused on building out its own AI agent products in-house. Decagon is privately held, so ServiceNow’s statement doesn’t point to any other listed company.
Palantir sells data analytics and AI software to government and commercial clients through Gotham, Foundry and its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP). Gotham serves government customers, Foundry targets commercial users, and AIP helps organizations put AI to work inside their operations. Its pitch centers on AI sovereignty, the idea that customers can deploy AI while keeping full control of their data.
ServiceNow sells workflow software and Salesforce sells customer-relationship software, both on recurring subscriptions with their own AI agent products. On the product side, ServiceNow’s AI Control Tower governs and deploys enterprise AI agents, while Salesforce builds its pitch around Agentforce. Those subscription models give ServiceNow and Salesforce steadier revenue, yet ServiceNow stock and Salesforce stock are sliding with the rest of the AI-linked group.
Palantir’s bullish thesis rests on its government and commercial AI demand. Palantir serves U.S. defense, intelligence and civilian agencies, international governments and a rapidly expanding base of U.S. commercial enterprises. That diversity gives Palantir more than one source of AI spending to draw from as customers build out their own systems.
The skeptics could read the selloff differently. In the bear case, software tied to AI spending is being marked down with the rest of the AI trade, and Palantir stock has little cushion when sentiment turns. Despite strong customer demand, Palantir shares are falling alongside ServiceNow stock and Salesforce stock.
AI Financing Fears Test Software Premiums
Investors should watch to see if the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF narrows its gap with the Invesco QQQ Trust, which could signal that the software rotation is easing. Palantir’s government and commercial AI demand gives the company a fundamental anchor while that rotation plays out.
The open variable for Palantir, ServiceNow and Salesforce is the depth of the rotation out of AI-linked stocks, with ServiceNow also committed to organic growth after its Decagon statement. A conservative approach fits a selloff driven by financing concerns across the AI trade, so owners of Palantir stock, ServiceNow stock and Salesforce stock should keep their position sizes moderate.
